title: Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Inferior Mesenteric Artery

sections.Introduction:
The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) arises from the abdominal aorta a few inches inferior to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). After originating at the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3), the IMA courses slightly lateral to the abdominal aorta, posterior to the 3rd part of the duodenum. Embryologically, the IMA supplies the hindgut, which comprises the distal portion of the intestinal tract. The hindgut consists of the distal 1/3 of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and superior segment of the rectum. The IMA classically terminates in 3 branches. From proximal to distal, these branches are the left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal arteries. Arterial arcades carry blood from the IMA branches to the colon.[1][2][3] See "Anatomy, Abdomen and Pelvis: Superior Mesenteric Artery" for further information.

The marginal artery of Drummond is a collateral pathway connecting the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial systems. The anastomotic network begins with the ascending branch of the ileocolic artery, the inferior-most branch of the SMA. The ileocolic artery connects with the right colic artery through the ascending and descending branches of the right colic artery. The network also connects with the right and left branches of the middle colic artery, the ascending and descending branches of the left colic artery, and the sigmoid branches of the IMA, which terminate in the superior rectal artery. The marginal artery often courses close to the bowel wall or within the mesentery. Less than 50% of the population has a fully continuous collateral network around the splenic flexure, known as Griffith point. Collateral insufficiency between the left branch of the middle colic artery and the ascending left colic artery may result in colonic ischemia when bowel surgery disrupts collateral circulation or occlusive disease restricts arterial blood flow.
sections.Structure and Function:
The IMA arises from the aorta at the L3 level and has 3 main branches: the left colic, sigmoid, and superior rectal arteries (see Image. Distal Colon and Rectal Arterial Supply). Variability in the origins of the 3 branches has been reported. The left colic and sigmoid arteries arise independently in 41.2% of patients and share a common trunk in 44.7% of patients. Approximately 5% of patients lack a left colic artery.[5] The IMA supplies blood to the distal 1/3 of the transverse colon, the descending colon, and the proximal 2/3 of the rectum.

[Figure] Distal Colon and Rectal Arterial Supply. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal colon via sigmoid branches and continues as the superior rectal artery. The marginal artery of Drummond forms a collateral arcade along the colon. The middle and superior hemorrhoidal arteries support rectal blood flow. sections.Blood Supply and Lymphatics:
The IMA arises from the anterolateral aspect of the left side of the aorta. The origin lies inferior to the renal arteries and superior to the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries, usually at the L3 level. The branches of the IMA include the left colic artery, which courses retroperitoneally and supplies the descending colon; the sigmoid arteries, which perfuse the sigmoid colon; and the superior rectal artery, the terminal branch of the IMA at the pelvic brim. The superior rectal artery supplies the upper rectum. All IMA branches have multiple fine arterial arcades that provide circulation to the left colon in segments. The inferior mesenteric vein accompanies the IMA. The inferior mesenteric vein does not drain into the inferior vena cava but instead empties into the splenic vein. The splenic vein then contributes to the portal venous system through the formation of the portal vein.

Left Colic Artery

The 1st branch of the IMA is the left colic artery. The left colic artery supplies the distal 1/3 of the transverse colon and the entire descending colon. After branching from the IMA, the left colic artery courses anterior to the left ureter, the left internal spermatic vessels in male individuals, and the psoas major before dividing into ascending and descending branches. The ascending branch courses anterior to the left kidney before entering the mesentery of the transverse colon. This branch supplies the distal 1/3 of the transverse colon and the proximal descending colon. The descending branch courses inferiorly from the bifurcation to supply the distal descending colon. This branch anastomoses with the superior sigmoid artery.

Sigmoid Arteries

The sigmoid arteries anastomose with the descending branch of the left colic artery and contribute to the blood supply of the distal descending colon. The sigmoid arteries typically consist of 2 to 4 branches, with the superior branch known as the superior sigmoid artery. The branches course in an inferior, oblique, and leftward direction, crossing over the psoas major, left ureter, and left internal spermatic vessels.

sections.Physiologic Variants: Anatomical variation of the IMA occurs through duplication or absence of the IMA, absence of the left colic artery, shortening of the IMA, or branching of the left colic and sigmoid arteries from a common origin. The arc of Riolan is a variant involving an anastomotic connection between the SMA and IMA.[6]
sections.Surgical Considerations:
The IMA is usually ligated near its origin from the abdominal aorta during a left hemicolectomy. The optimal location for IMA ligation during rectal resection remains debated. A high-tie approach involves ligation of the IMA near its aortic origin, whereas a low-tie approach involves ligation distal to the origin of the left colic artery. Ligation of the IMA near its origin significantly decreases perfusion to the splenic flexure.[7][8][9][10][11][12] Reduced perfusion can contribute to anastomotic leakage after restorative rectal resection with anastomosis. Adequate perfusion on both sides of the colonic anastomosis must be ensured.

During abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, the IMA may be reimplanted into the aortic graft when adequate collateral circulation is absent. After aortic clamping, the IMA may continue to perfuse the colon through collateral vessels and can be ligated when collateral perfusion is adequate. Postoperatively, rectal bleeding and abdominal pain may indicate ischemic colitis when the IMA is not reimplanted. Urgent sigmoidoscopy is recommended when ischemic bowel is suspected.[13][14][15][16]
sections.Clinical Significance:
Horseshoe kidney is a congenital anomaly affecting approximately 1 in 400 to 600 people and occurs more frequently in men. During embryonic development, the kidneys fuse and ascend from the pelvis toward their abdominal positions. The fused kidneys become trapped below the IMA and consequently remain in the lower abdomen. Horseshoe kidneys are usually asymptomatic and typically do not require treatment.[17]

Mesenteric arterial thrombosis typically occurs in patients with hypercoagulability or cardiac arrhythmias, resulting in arterial occlusion, most commonly involving the proximal SMA. Acute abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea are common presenting features. IMA occlusion may occur but is rare because of the smaller caliber of the blood vessel.[18]
